narr: Welcome to this comprehensive study guide for the Introduction to Engineering course. This guide covers the first four weeks of the course, including all questions, assignments, terms, formulas, and rules from lectures, labs, the syllabus, and three textbooks.
The course is taught by Dr. Mohammad Reza Bahrami and Ibrokhimjon Khamidov, following a Project-Based Learning approach where teams work on one system throughout the semester.

narr: Here's a breakdown of the first four weeks of the course. Each week focuses on a specific topic with corresponding lectures, labs, and textbook chapters.
Week 1 introduces engineering as a profession, covering its cultural, historical, and economic aspects.
Week 1 explores systems thinking, focusing on how systems consist of interacting elements, processes, and stakeholders.
Week 2 continues with systems thinking, introducing process flow diagrams and how different perspectives can lead to different interpretations of the same system.
Week 4 covers problem framing and modeling, teaching how to transform informal observations into well-defined engineering problems and identify variables.
The course is built on three main textbooks. Each serves a specific purpose in your engineering education.
First, Kosky's 'Exploring Engineering: An Introduction to Engineering and Design' is the primary text, explicitly referenced in all four lectures.
Second, Moaveni's 'Engineering Fundamentals: An Introduction to Engineering' covers the profession, ethics, design, and units of measurement.
Third, Dym's 'Engineering Design: A Project-Based Introduction' focuses on problem framing, including project goals, constraints, and functions.

data.title: Course Structure and Workload
data.subtitle: Understanding the course requirements and expectations

narr: The course has a total workload of 120 hours, distributed as follows: 30 hours of lectures, 30 hours of in-class team project work, and 60 hours of independent study.

There are no prerequisites, and the course is open to all first-year students. What's expected is working with basic quantitative logic, active participation in teamwork, and clear communication in English.

data.heading: Intended Learning Outcomes
bullets: ILO-1 (Understand) — Explain that engineering models are purposeful simplifications of complex systems, and describe how assumptions and approximations shape a model's usefulness and limitations.
ILO-2 (Apply) — Apply basic quantitative reasoning (demand and capacity, rates and flows, order-of-magnitude estimates) to characterize the behavior of a real system from incomplete data.
ILO-3 (Analyze) — Analyze system dynamics (delays, queues, capacity, bottlenecks) and use simple simulations under uncertainty.

ILO-4 (Evaluate) — Evaluate trade-offs between competing objectives (efficiency, cost, fairness, accessibility) and justify a design decision taking technical, ethical and stakeholder considerations into account.
ILO-5 (Apply) — Collaborate effectively in a team throughout the semester project and present models, assumptions and decisions clearly in writing and orally.

narr: The course has five intended learning outcomes, each mapped to specific Bloom's taxonomy levels and ASIIN competencies.
First, you'll learn to understand that engineering models are simplifications of complex systems and how assumptions affect their usefulness.
Second, you'll apply quantitative reasoning to understand real system behavior with incomplete data.
Third, you'll analyze system dynamics and use simulations under uncertainty.
Fourth, you'll evaluate trade-offs between competing objectives and justify design decisions considering technical, ethical, and stakeholder factors.
Finally, you'll learn to collaborate effectively in teams and present your work clearly in writing and orally.
Your grade in this course will be determined by three main components.
Weekly mini projects account for 30% of your grade and consist of reports and presentations.
The midterm exam is a written exam on paper worth 30% of your grade.
The final exam is also a written exam on paper, worth 40% of your grade.
Each assessment component maps to specific learning outcomes, ensuring you're evaluated on all aspects of the course.
The course uses a straightforward grading scale. Scores from 90 to 100 earn an A, indicating excellent performance.
Scores between 75 and 89 receive a B, which is good.
Scores from 60 to 74 are considered satisfactory, earning a C.
Below 60 points results in a failing grade of D.
